blocks.h: Why check `p and …` first inside the IPv4 test?
p: An empty field (from `"1..1.1"` or a trailing dot) would make `p[0]` raise IndexError and `int('')` raise ValueError. The leading `p and` short-circuits on an empty string and the whole field is rejected, so the validator never crashes on malformed input.

p: `[4,14,2]` = `[0100, 1110, 0010]`. Only the lowest 4 bit positions can be nonzero; the other 28 contribute 0:

blocks.h: Why count bits instead of comparing pairs?
p: Hamming distance sums over bit positions, and for each position the contribution of all pairs is independent. Comparing all pairs costs O(n²·32); counting ones per position costs O(32·n), and `c·(n−c)` counts exactly the pairs with different bits at that position.

477.takeaway: Total Hamming distance = Σ over bit positions of ones × zeros.

p: After you pick, the roles swap: the opponent is now the player to move on the smaller range, and `dp[...]` is their best advantage. Your advantage is therefore your pick minus theirs. Because both play optimally, a single table of differences replaces separate tables for each player.

bullets: Space: O(n²), reducible to O(n) with a rolling diagonal.

486.takeaway: Predict the Winner: interval DP of score difference; take an end, subtract the opponent's best difference on the rest.

blocks.h: Why does the zigzag need reversal only on every other diagonal?
p: The traversal alternates direction. Collecting in row order gives one direction for free (up-right to down-left, i.e. top to bottom). The opposite direction is that list reversed. Parity of `d` decides which one is needed, starting with `d = 0` (a single cell) going 'up'.

bullets: Space: O(m·n) for the grouping; a direct simulation with a direction flag uses O(1) extra.

498.takeaway: Group cells by i + j, then read the groups in order, reversing every other one.

blocks.h: Why does the parity trick work?
p: Before the single element, every pair occupies indices (even, odd). After it, pairs shift to (odd, even). Checking an even index `mid` against `mid + 1` tells which side we are on: equal → still in the unshifted region, so the single is to the right; different → the shift has already happened (or mid is the single), so it is at `mid` or to the left.

bullets: XOR of all elements also works in O(n) but ignores the sorted property.

540.takeaway: Binary search on pair alignment: round mid down to even, and compare with its right neighbour to see whether the pairs have shifted.

blocks.h: Why do we return the height but record the diameter separately?
p: A path through a node uses BOTH of its children, but a path continuing up to the parent can use only one of them. So the value passed upward must be the single-branch height, while the two-branch sum is recorded as a candidate answer. Mixing the two is the classic mistake.
The longest path need not pass through the root. Computing `best` at every node covers all possible highest points.

543.takeaway: Diameter = max over nodes of (left height + right height); return the height upward, keep the sum in a nonlocal.

while r > l and boxes[r] == boxes[r-1]: r -= 1; k += 1
Absorbs equal neighbours into k so identical runs are never split
Option 1: remove boxes[r] with its k attached boxes now, scoring (k+1)²
Option 2: for a same-coloured box i, first clear the middle i+1..r−1, so boxes[r] joins i's group

p: For `boxes = [1,3,1]` the best plan is to remove the 3 first (1 point) and then the two 1s together (4 points):
bullets: For the full example `[1, 3, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 3, 1]` the memoized search returns `23` after 27 distinct calls (cached repeats don't count).

p: Joining boxes of the same colour is rewarded quadratically, but the best join may combine boxes that are far apart after the middle is removed. Without `k` the recursion cannot tell how many same-coloured boxes are already waiting beside boxes[r], so subproblems on a plain range [l, r] are not self-contained. The extra parameter makes the subproblem complete, giving O(n³) states.

bullets: Time: O(n⁴) worst case: O(n³) states (l, r, k) with an O(n) loop each.

546.takeaway: Remove Boxes: memoized interval DP with an extra count k of equal-coloured boxes attached to the right end.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Longest consecutive run going DOWN from node with values increasing (+1 each step), and the longest with values decreasing (−1 each step)
Returning a pair from a recursion
Child extends the increasing run: `inc = ci + 1`
A path that bends at this node: one arm increasing, the other decreasing (they share the node, so subtract 1)

p: Tree `[2,1,3]`: node 2 with children 1 and 3. Post-order:
bullets: At 2: the child 1 extends `dec` (2 → 1) and the child 3 extends `inc` (2 → 3), so the path 1 → 2 → 3 has length 2 + 2 − 1 = 3.

blocks.h: Why is `inc + dec - 1` the path length?
p: Going down one child, the values go up by 1 each step; going down the other child they go down by 1 each step. Read from one leaf, through the node, to the other leaf, the whole path is monotone (…, node−1, node, node+1, …). `inc` counts the node plus the increasing arm, `dec` counts the node plus the decreasing arm, so the node is counted twice.

549.takeaway: Track the longest increasing and decreasing runs down from each node; a path bending at a node has length inc + dec − 1.
